slides.0.title: Diploma sparkling tasting and essays
slides.0.subtitle: SAT demonstration, NV blind clues and MW essay templates
slides.1.title: SAT demonstration: a typical Brut NV
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Appearance
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Clear, medium intensity, lemon; fine, persistent, continuous bead of bubbles (fineness and persistence are key traditional-method clues). Note: this page is a generic demonstration, not a tasting record of a specific wine; the exact fields and descriptors follow the latest official WSET specification
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Nose
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Clean, medium(+) intensity, developing; primary green apple, lemon and white blossom, with autolytic brioche, toast and almond, and a little honey and dried fruit. Method: condition and intensity first, then layers: primary → winemaking (autolysis/oxidation) → age
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Palate
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Dry (Brut, roughly in the 6–12 g/L band), high acidity, medium alcohol, medium(+) body; creamy, fine mousse; medium(+) flavour intensity consistent with the nose and a chalky minerality; long finish. Call out how acidity, mousse and dosage balance each other rather than listing them separately
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Conclusions
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Quality: very good. Organise the reasons with BLIC: balance (acidity, dosage, body), length, intensity, complexity (primary + autolytic + a little development). Readiness and potential: drinkable now with room to age. A conclusion needs reasons leading to a judgement, not just a label
slides.1.content: Exam vocabulary and format may be updated; this lesson only shows how to turn observation into an evidence-based judgement. Keep the current official SAT template to hand.
slides.2.title: Blind-comparison clues for NV
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Chardonnay-led vs Pinot Noir/Meunier-led
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Chardonnay-led: citrus, white blossom, minerality and a linear acid line; Pinot Noir-led: red fruit, body and structure; Meunier-led: round fruit, drinks early (Levels 1 and 3). Clues are tendencies, not identification — use “more likely … because …”
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Clues to reserve-wine share
slides.2.highlights.1.content: A deeper colour, nuts and caramel and a broad texture may point to a higher reserve share or longer ageing, but may equally be post-disgorgement age or oxidative winemaking; offer at least two explanations and say how to tell them apart (is the fruit still fresh, is autolysis marked?)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Dosage and sweetness clues
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Brut Nature / Extra Brut: sharp acid, leaner texture, needs ripe fruit; Brut: the balance point for most NVs; Extra Dry and above: clearly sweet and needing acid to carry it. Judge sweetness together with acidity and body, and remember the ±3 g/L tolerance
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Telling it from other sparkling wines
slides.2.highlights.3.content: Autolysis, high acid, fine mousse: traditional method from a cool origin (Champagne, England). Riper fruit and lower acid: a warmer origin (such as Cava or some New World). Clear floral and fruity notes with no autolysis: tank method (such as Prosecco). Decide method first, origin second, grape last (ch-l3-3)
slides.2.content: Blind-tasting logic: observation → inference → counter-evidence → conclusion; every inference needs evidence.
slides.3.title: MW essay 1: does Champagne still need dosage in a warming climate?
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Define first
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Dosage is the liqueur d’expédition added after disgorgement to balance acidity and shape style and to set the sweetness category. Define the question: “still need dosage” meaning conventional Brut-level dosage, or zero dosage? A loose definition makes everything after it drift
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Arguments for and against, with evidence
slides.3.highlights.1.content: For lowering: earlier harvests, higher potential alcohol and lower total acidity (IWC citing CIVC, 2019) give riper fruit and fuller texture, needing less sugar. For keeping: acidity is also falling, some years still have residual acid to balance, low dosage amplifies bitterness and leanness, and consumer preference and price position matter. Tie each point to facts built earlier (ch-l3-1, ch-l3-2)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Alternative tools
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Dosage is not the only tool: adjust harvest timing, skip MLF, use more high-acid base wines in the reserve, manage canopy and fertiliser (ch-l3-1, ch-l3-2), research new varieties such as Voltis. Compare the cost and style consequences of compensating with dosage against managing at source
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Position and conclusion template
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Sample conclusion (adapt it): “As the climate warms, dosage shifts from compensating for acid to fine-tuning balance: most conventional NVs will still need it, while zero dosage becomes more viable in ripe, long-aged vintage wines with enough acidity. Limits: this rests on trend descriptions from around 2019 and expert views from the region; houses differ in stock and target customers, so the conclusion should not be generalised.”
slides.3.content: MW marking looks for a clear position, real evidence and honest limits, not how many numbers you can recite.
slides.4.title: MW essays 2 and 3: reserve wine and growers versus Grandes Marques
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Essay 2: how the reserve system shapes NV style
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Skeleton: (1) function — consistency across years and a buffer against short crops (Comité Champagne and the specification); (2) stylistic consequence — maturity, complexity, steadier acid and texture, but possibly muted vintage character; (3) climate and market — older high-acid wines top up warm vintages, stock pressure; (4) limits — shares vary by house and are not public, so no single number should carry the argument. Evidence from ch-l3-2 and ch-l3-5
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Essay 3: grower Champagne versus Grandes Marques
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Axes of comparison: expression of place (single village and vintage, where RM can shine) versus blending and consistency (where large NMs shine); scale and stocks (depth of reserves); price and value; distribution and brand. Codes say nothing about quality (DGCCRF), so argue from specific attributes rather than concluding from an RM/NM label
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Time and structure
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Suggested structure (for practice): 2–3 sentences of definition and position; 2–3 argument paragraphs (claim, evidence, implication); one paragraph for the other side; a conclusion with limits. Spend two minutes outlining before writing. Actual formats, word counts and time limits follow the latest official IMW specification
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Self-check list
slides.4.highlights.3.content: Does every number carry a year and source? Have contested numbers been treated as settled? Did you separate specification from customary description? Are limits stated? Are other people’s claims (LVMH researchers, IWC) marked as claims rather than facts? Before the exam, check every format and requirement against the latest official WSET/IMW specifications
slides.4.content: These three are practice templates, not official questions; rewrite them in your own words.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
In a blind tasting, which clue most strongly points to traditional method with lees ageing?
A. Pronounced grapey and floral aromas with no autolysis
B. Autolytic brioche, toast and almond with a fine, persistent mousse
Autolytic notes and a fine mousse are clues to bottle fermentation and lees ageing; tank-method wines usually keep primary fruit and floral aromas.
In an essay on whether Champagne still needs dosage in a warming climate, which approach is best?
A. Define dosage, argue both sides with evidence, then give a qualified conclusion
B. Just write that sweetness does not matter
C. List as many numbers as possible without sources
MW marking rewards definition, evidence, the other side and honest limits, not recited figures.
When comparing grower Champagne (RM) with large houses (NM), which statement is most appropriate?
A. RM is always better than NM
B. NM is always better than RM
C. The code does not imply quality; argue from concrete attributes (expression of place, consistency, stocks, value)
D. They are made identically and need no comparison
The DGCCRF states that the code does not presuppose the maker’s quality; the differences are in business model and scale.
